newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH C.BANK SAYS LOAN LOSS PROVISIONS SUFFICIENT.
newsitem.headline: CZECH C.BANK SAYS LOAN LOSS PROVISIONS SUFFICIENT.

text.p: Czech banks appear sufficiently provisioned against losses and the impact on loan portfolios from recent floods and a weaker crown should not be "dramatic", the Czech National Bank (CNB) said on Thursday.

"This can be an unpleasant situation for the banks. What will be the size of the problem and how this will affect the position of the banking sector is now hard to predict," CNB spokesman Martin Svehla told Reuters.
"For sure, this is not good news for the banks."
Asked if the central bank thought commercial banks were well provisioned to cover potential losses from floods and affects of the weaker crown, Svehla said the situation appeared sound.

"Based on figures we have, and also the opinions of auditors, I think this (negative effect from floods and the crown weakening) must not be something dramatic, but certainly bankers are used to being sceptical."

He said high interest rates resulting from the crown's sharp drop in the spring would "certainly" cut into banks' bottom lines, as will lagging loan repayment from firms devastated by July floods in the east of the country.

The latest CNB data show the total volume of total "loss" loans considered unrecoverable in the banking sector had risen slightly to about 224 billion crowns from 221 billion in the 12 months ending May 31.
But as a percentage of the overall credit portfolios of the banking sector, unrecoverable loans dipped to 20.2 percent at the end of May, from 22.8 percent the previous year.
"This is influenced by the fact that we have withdrawn some (banking) licences, and in a way withdrew a part of the bad assets," Svehla said.
"On the other hand the opposite tendency is that the volume of other classes of bad loans are falling over time."

Overall loans considered "classified" by the Czech National Bank at domestic and foreign banks registered in the Czech Republic fell as a percentage of total credit to 33.1 percent at the end of May from 37.22 percent last May.
"Classified" credits include all new loans for a probationary period and any credit deemed non-standard, doubtful, or a total writeoff.
The total volume of provisions created against classified loans rose to nearly 93 billion crowns from 79 billion crowns at the end of May, year-on-year.
The central bank shut or took over managament of several ailing small private banks in 1996 as poor risk assessment and losses in the the post-Communist economic transformation made them illiquid.
For the remaining small banks in need of stabilisation, the central bank initiated a bad debt buy-back programme late last year. Five banks have participated in this.
Svehla said the consolidation programme had been successful in keeping these banks out of liquidity trouble.
"Yes, for sure it had its logic in that it granted a kind of help towards small banks which participated in financing the transition of the Czech economy and were faced with losses due to this."
